seoDescription: Learn how to build multi-page applications in SolidJS with the Solid Router. This tutorial guides you through installing the official routing package, setting up the main `Router` component, and defining individual page routes. You'll see how to create distinct page components for your home and cart pages and how to display them based on the current URL. Discover the difference between standard `<a>` tags and Solid's special `A` component for seamless, client-side navigation without full page reloads.

chapters.title: Introducing & Installing Solid Router
chapters.description: Covers the need for client-side routing in SolidJS and walks through the process of installing the Solid Router package via npm.

chapters.title: How Front-End Routing Works
chapters.description: Explains the core concept of client-side routing, where components are swapped in the browser without full page reloads, and reviews the setup steps from the official documentation.

chapters.title: Implementing the Router and First Route
chapters.description: Details how to wrap the root application with the `Router` component and then define the main `Routes` outlet and the first `Route` for the home page.

chapters.title: Creating the Home Page Component
chapters.description: Shows how to create a dedicated `Home` page component, move the existing page content into it, and correctly import dependencies.

chapters.title: Adding a Cart Page Route
chapters.description: Demonstrates how to add a second route for a shopping cart, create the corresponding `Cart.jsx` page component, and register it in the router configuration.

chapters.title: Building and Debugging the Cart Page
chapters.description: Details the creation of the cart page's view, fixes a component import error, and manually navigates to both the home and cart pages to verify the routes are working correctly.

chapters.title: The Problem with Native Anchor Tags
chapters.description: Explains why standard `<a>` tags cause undesirable full-page reloads and demonstrates this behavior using the browser's network inspector.

chapters.title: Using the Link Component for SPA Navigation
chapters.description: Replaces standard anchor tags with Solid Router's `A` component to enable true single-page application navigation and previews the next topic on data fetching.

## Introduction to Solid Router Solid Router is a separate package used to create multi-page SolidJS applications. It enables **client-side routing**, where navigation is handled entirely in the browser by swapping components instead of fetching new HTML pages from a server. ## Installation & Setup Setting up the router involves a few key steps: 1. **Install the package** from your terminal: ```bash npm install @solidjs/router ``` 2. **Wrap your App**: In your `src/index.jsx` file, import the `Router` and wrap your root `` component with it. This makes routing functionality available throughout your entire application. ```jsx import { render } from 'solid-js/web'; import { Router } from '@solidjs/router'; import App from './App'; render(() => , document.getElementById('root')); ``` ## Defining Routes Inside your main `App` component, you define where page content should appear and which components correspond to which URLs. - Use the **``** component as a wrapper for all your individual routes. - Define each page using a **``** component with two main props: - `path`: The URL path for the route (e.g., `"/"`, `"/cart"`). - `component`: The page component to render for that path (e.g., `{Home}`). > [!TIP] > It's a good practice to organize page-level components in a dedicated `src/pages` directory (e.g., `src/pages/Home.jsx`, `src/pages/Cart.jsx`). ## Navigating Between Pages To navigate between routes without triggering a full page reload, you must use the special link component provided by Solid Router. > [!IMPORTANT] > Do not use standard `` tags for internal navigation. They send a new request to the server, which defeats the purpose of a Single-Page Application (SPA). Instead, use the `` component. - Import the **``** component from `@solidjs/router`. - Use it just like a regular anchor tag, with an `href` prop. **Example:** ```jsx import { A } from '@solidjs/router'; function Header() { return (
Home Cart
); } ``` The `` component intercepts the user's click, prevents the default browser behavior, and instructs the router to render the correct page component.

## How Front-End Routing Works

And it's important to note as well that these pages and routes are purely going to be front-end pages and routes. We won't ever be sending requests to the server for different HTML pages. Whenever we go to a different route, if we click a link in the site, the way front-end routers work is that all of the routing is handled in a browser.

So imagine we click on a link to go to a different route in the site, for example, to forward slash about. Then what the solid router will do is look at that route and say, okay, well for that route, I'm going to swap the current component in the page for the about component. And the HTML page is still the same HTML page, we're just swapping out the content inside it depending on the route that we visit. I hope that makes sense. And that's pretty much the way any front-end router works, whether it be Solid, React, Vue, or something else.

Anyway, if we go back to the docs, we can see we need to do a couple of things. First, we need to wrap this router component which is imported from the solid router package around the root app component. ## The Problem with Native Anchor Tags
